title: The Three Body Problem and Assessment Design
author: The Last Analogue
summary: The Last Analogue uses Liu Cixin's fictional three-body problem, in which a civilization orbits three suns whose combined gravity produces no stable, predictable path, as an extended metaphor for the structural instability of course assessment design. The author identifies four comparable-strength forces acting on any assessment brief: industry expectations of job-readiness, institution-wide capability frameworks, course learning outcomes, and the constantly shifting capability of AI tools, and argues that treating all four as equally weighted produces genuine chaos, where the assessment task gets rewritten piecemeal by whichever stakeholder spoke most recently and its validity slowly erodes. Drawing on the real orbital-mechanics concept of Lagrange points, the piece describes a second option, treating CLOs and one other force as 'giants' with the course as a minor body orbiting between them, which produces stability but leaves the course perpetually reactive to forces it cannot influence. The proposed resolution is to deliberately declare course learning outcomes the dominant mass in the system, not because they are naturally permanent, but because a coordinator chooses to hold them fixed for the length of a teaching period, which converts competing pressures into constrained adjustments around a settled purpose rather than directionless pulls. The piece closes by rejecting the premise of a final solution altogether, arguing that assessment design, like a three-body system, can only be continuously navigated in motion, never solved once and for all.
points: The author maps Liu Cixin's fictional three-body problem onto assessment design, arguing that industry expectations, institutional frameworks, CLOs, and AI capability are comparable-strength forces that make unanchored assessment design structurally chaotic.

Leaving all four influences equally weighted produces the worst outcome: the assessment brief gets rewritten piecemeal by whichever stakeholder spoke most recently, and validity erodes because nothing was ever declared non-negotiable.

The 'two giants plus one minor body' configuration borrows the real concept of Lagrange points to describe a course that stays stable only by continuously repositioning itself relative to forces it can't control.

The recommended solution is to deliberately fix CLOs as the dominant mass, chosen rather than natural, which turns competing pressures into constrained adjustments around a settled purpose instead of directionless pulls.
The piece closes by rejecting the idea of a permanent solution altogether: like a three-body system, assessment design can only be continuously navigated, not solved once and for all.
quotes: Every suite of course assessments often has to answer to several moving targets at once: an industry partner's sense of what counts as job-ready, an institution-wide capability framework, course learning outcomes, and, running underneath all of them, whatever the current generation of AI tools can already do.

Long Stable Eras alternate with Chaotic Eras that arrive without warning and can destroy a civilisation outright. The Trisolarans respond by dehydrating themselves, reducing their bodies to something inert and storable, and waiting out the chaos until a stable window opens again.

Whichever voice is loudest that semester wins, so the task ends up shaped by pressure rather than by design, and the coordinator spends the semester firefighting instead of coordinating. Because nothing was ever declared non-negotiable, validity erodes, until someone asks what the task is actually evidence of.
This is the restricted three-body problem, and it produces Lagrange points: positions where a body too small to influence the two giants can still hold a relatively stable relationship with them.

CLOs earn that priority by choice, not by nature. The coordinator declares them the first claim on the design for the teaching period. This is where agency enters: the giants outside a course aren't yours to move, but what gets priority inside it is.

There will be no closed-form solution that makes assessment design stable once and for all. Fixing the CLOs as the central mass gives you a system that can be continuously rebuilt (subject to resourcing!) without losing its educational purpose.
